BIOCHEMISTRY__Renal & Electrolytes:
The U&E — sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine (± bicarbonate) — is the commonest biochemistry test. It assesses renal function, hydration, electrolyte and acid–base status in almost every acutely unwell patient.
1What it measures
🧂Sodium (Na⁺)
A marker of water balance, not salt content. Abnormalities usually reflect too much or too little water (see the Na⁺ tab).
⚡Potassium (K⁺)
A tight, life-threatening range — high or low K⁺ causes arrhythmia. Always the first number to check on a U&E.
💧Urea
A nitrogenous waste product. Rises with renal impairment but also, disproportionately, with dehydration and an upper GI bleed.
🫘Creatinine
From muscle — the main marker of GFR / renal function. Varies with muscle mass (low in the frail/cachectic). Drives the eGFR.
2Urea vs creatinine
↑ Urea >> creatinine (high ratio)→Pre-renal — dehydration/hypovolaemia, or an upper GI bleed (absorbed protein).
↑ Urea & creatinine (proportionate)→Intrinsic renal or post-renal (obstruction) — work up the AKI › / CKD ›.
↓ Urea→Liver failure (reduced synthesis), low-protein diet, or over-hydration.
3Potassium — the emergency electrolyte
🔺Hyperkalaemia (>5.5)
AKI/CKD, K⁺-sparing diuretics, ACEi/ARB, Addison’s, acidosis, or a haemolysed sample. ECG: tall tented T waves → wide QRS.
🔻Hypokalaemia (<3.5)
GI loss (vomiting/diarrhoea), diuretics, Conn’s, alkalosis. ECG: flat T waves, U waves.
4Typical adult ranges (check local lab)
Na⁺ 135–145 mmol/LK⁺ 3.5–5.3 mmol/LUrea 2.5–7.8 mmol/LCreatinine 60–110 µmol/LBicarbonate 22–29 mmol/L
🚩
Hyperkalaemia ≥6.0 mmol/L, or any K⁺ with ECG changes, is an emergency → IV calcium gluconate (cardioprotection), then insulin + dextrose and salbutamol to shift K⁺, and treat the cause. Persistent hyperkalaemia may need a potassium binder (patiromer / sodium zirconium cyclosilicate), and refractory or oliguric cases need dialysis. A haemolysed sample can falsely raise K⁺ — repeat if unexpected, but never delay treating a genuine high K⁺.
📷 Image placeholder — the hyperkalaemia ECG progression (tall tented T waves → flattened P → widened QRS → sine wave) alongside a U&E interpretation flow.
🎓 Exam pearl. Sodium = water balance. A high urea:creatinine ratio → pre-renal (dehydration) or an upper GI bleed. Potassium is the killer — get an ECG and treat. Creatinine tracks GFR but depends on muscle mass (see the eGFR tab).
eGFR estimates the GFR from creatinine (with age and sex, CKD-EPI equation). CKD is then staged by GFR (G) and albuminuria (A) — the KDIGO G/A categories — and requires an abnormality persisting for ≥3 months.
1eGFR — how to read it
  • Estimated from creatinine (CKD-EPI, race-free), reported per 1.73 m².
  • Unreliable in AKI (non-steady state), extremes of muscle mass, pregnancy and acute illness — interpret creatinine trend instead.
2GFR categories (G)
G1 ≥90 (+ damage)G2 60–89G3a 45–59G3b 30–44G4 15–29G5 <15 (failure)
3Albuminuria categories (A)
A1 ACR <3 mg/mmolA2 3–30 (moderate)A3 >30 (severe)
Measured on a urine albumin:creatinine ratio (ACR) — the preferred marker of kidney damage.
4Diagnosis & significance
  • CKD = GFR <60 or markers of damage (ACR ≥3, haematuria, structural/histological) for ≥3 months. CKD ›
  • Combine G and A (the KDIGO heat map): higher categories → greater risk of progression and cardiovascular events.
  • Refer for eGFR <30 (G4–5), ACR ≥70, ACR ≥30 with haematuria, or a rapid decline.
  • Slow progression with BP control, an ACEi/ARB for proteinuria, and an SGLT2 inhibitor (e.g. dapagliflozin) — renoprotective in albuminuric CKD.
🚩
A low eGFR in an acutely unwell patient may be AKI, not CKD — eGFR is invalid when creatinine is not in steady state. Distinguish acute from chronic: check the baseline, and look for chronicity (small kidneys on USS, anaemia, renal bone disease). AKI ›
📷 Image placeholder — the KDIGO G/A heat-map grid (green→red) mapping GFR categories against albuminuria categories.
🎓 Exam pearl. CKD is staged by G (GFR) and A (ACR) and needs ≥3 months. eGFR is invalid in AKI. Use the ACR for albuminuria; combined G3b–5 / A3 carries the highest risk and prompts referral.
Acute kidney injury (AKI) is an abrupt fall in kidney function, defined and staged by KDIGO using the creatinine rise and urine output. Always ask: pre-renal, intrinsic or post-renal?
1KDIGO definition (any one)
  • Creatinine rise ≥26 µmol/L within 48 h, or
  • Creatinine ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days, or
  • Urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥6 h.
2Staging
1️⃣Stage 1
Creatinine 1.5–1.9× baseline (or ≥26 rise); UO <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 h.
2️⃣Stage 2
Creatinine 2.0–2.9× baseline; UO <0.5 for ≥12 h.
3️⃣Stage 3
Creatinine ≥3× baseline (or ≥354 µmol/L) or RRT; UO <0.3 for ≥24 h or anuria ≥12 h.
3Causes — pre / intrinsic / post
Pre-renal (commonest)→Hypovolaemia, sepsis, hypotension, cardiorenal/hepatorenal; NSAIDs and ACEi/ARB (haemodynamic).
Intrinsic→ATN (ischaemia, toxins, contrast, rhabdomyolysis), glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis, vasculitis.
Post-renal→Obstruction — stones, prostate, pelvic tumour — exclude with a renal ultrasound.
4Management principles
  • Assess and restore volume; treat the underlying cause (esp. sepsis).
  • Stop nephrotoxics — NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB, gentamicin, contrast; review drug doses.
  • Catheterise / ultrasound to exclude obstruction; monitor K⁺, fluid balance and acid–base.
  • Dipstick the urine — blood + protein suggests an intrinsic/glomerular cause (nephritis/vasculitis) needing urgent nephrology. Apply sick-day rules — hold metformin, ACEi/ARB, diuretics and NSAIDs during the acute illness.
🚩
Urgent dialysis (RRT) is indicated for the AEIOU refractory to medical therapy: Acidosis (severe), Electrolytes (refractory hyperkalaemia), Intoxication, Overload (pulmonary oedema), Uraemia (encephalopathy or pericarditis). AKI ›
🎓 Exam pearl. AKI (KDIGO) = creatinine ≥26 in 48 h, or ≥1.5× in 7 days, or UO <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h. Split causes pre / intrinsic / post; stop nephrotoxics and exclude obstruction (USS). Dialyse for AEIOU.
Sodium disorders are disorders of WATER balance. The work-up hinges on volume status and osmolality; and the speed of correction is a safety issue — over-rapid correction causes osmotic demyelination.
1First steps in hyponatraemia
  • Exclude pseudohyponatraemia (hyperlipidaemia, paraproteins) and correct for hyperglycaemia.
  • Check serum osmolality (usually low), urine osmolality and urine sodium.
  • Assess volume status — this is the pivot of the whole work-up.
2Hyponatraemia by volume status
🏜️Hypovolaemic
Fluid loss. Urine Na <20 = extrarenal (D&V, sweating); >20 = renal loss (diuretics, Addison’s).
⚖️Euvolaemic
SIADH, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, primary polydipsia (dilute urine).
💧Hypervolaemic
Oedematous states: heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, renal failure.
3SIADH
Euvolaemic hyponatraemia + low serum osmolality + inappropriately concentrated urine (osm >100, urine Na >30), with normal thyroid and adrenal function.
Causes: CNS (stroke, meningitis), lung (small-cell), drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine), surgery/pain. Treat: fluid restriction and treat the cause; a vasopressin-receptor antagonist (tolvaptan) or demeclocycline is used for resistant cases. SIADH ›
4Hypernatraemia
Always a water deficit. Poor intake/dehydration, D&V, osmotic diuresis, or diabetes insipidus (dilute urine despite a high sodium).
Replace water (oral, or IV 5% dextrose / hypotonic saline) — slowly. Diabetes insipidus ›
5Correction limits (safety)
  • Hyponatraemia: raise the sodium by no more than ~8–10 mmol/L in 24 h (less in high-risk) — faster risks osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis).
  • Hypernatraemia: lower by ~10 mmol/L/24 h — too fast causes cerebral oedema.
🚩
Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, reduced GCS) needs hypertonic (3%) saline in small boluses under senior/critical-care guidance. Then monitor the sodium frequently — overcorrection → osmotic demyelination (a devastating locked-in syndrome).
📷 Image placeholder — the hyponatraemia work-up flow (osmolality → volume status → urine Na/osm) and the safe-correction-rate graph.
🎓 Exam pearl. Sodium = water. Assess volume status. SIADH = euvolaemic, low serum osm, concentrated urine, normal thyroid/adrenal → fluid restrict. Don’t correct Na >8–10 mmol/L per 24 h (osmotic demyelination). Hypernatraemia = water deficit, correct slowly.
Serum urate is a product of purine metabolism, excreted by the kidney. It is measured mainly in gout, in tumour lysis syndrome, and in pre-eclampsia — with important interpretation caveats.
1Causes of a raised urate
GoutTumour lysis syndromeCKDThiazide / loop diureticsAlcohol / high purine intakeMyeloproliferative disordersPre-eclampsia
2The gout timing caveat
Serum urate can be normal (or low) during an acute attack — so a normal level does not exclude gout.
Diagnose acute gout clinically or by joint aspirate — negatively birefringent, needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals. Recheck urate 4–6 weeks after the attack. Crystal arthropathies ›
3Other settings
Tumour lysis syndrome→↑urate, ↑K⁺, ↑phosphate, ↓calcium → AKI & arrhythmia. Oncological emergencies ›
Pre-eclampsia→A raised urate correlates with severity.
Urate stones→Radiolucent stones in persistent hyperuricaemia/aciduria. Renal stones ›
4Management context
  • Urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol; febuxostat) for recurrent gout, tophi or urate stones — start after the attack settles, under prophylactic cover.
  • Do not treat asymptomatic hyperuricaemia.
  • Tumour lysis: hydration and allopurinol (prevention) or rasburicase (treatment — contraindicated in G6PD deficiency, as it causes haemolysis).
🚩
A hot, swollen joint is septic arthritis until proven otherwise — do not assume gout; aspirate for crystals AND Gram stain/culture. In tumour lysis syndrome, hydration is the backbone — allopurinol at low or intermediate risk, rasburicase at high risk or in established TLS (never both) — and monitor K⁺/phosphate/calcium and renal function.
🎓 Exam pearl. Serum urate can be normal in an acute gout attack — diagnose by aspirate (negatively birefringent MSU crystals) and recheck later. Rasburicase for high-risk or established tumour lysis; allopurinol at lower risk. Do not treat asymptomatic hyperuricaemia, and never assume a hot joint is gout without excluding sepsis.
BIOCHEMISTRY__Liver & Pancreas:
The LFTs — bilirubin, ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, albumin (plus clotting) — are read as a pattern: hepatocellular vs cholestatic, with albumin and PT/INR reflecting the liver’s synthetic function.
1What it measures
🔥ALT & AST
Hepatocellular enzymes (hepatocyte damage). ALT is more liver-specific; an AST:ALT ratio >2 suggests alcohol.
🚧ALP & GGT
Cholestatic enzymes. ALP rises in cholestasis (and bone); a raised GGT confirms the ALP is hepatic.
🟡Bilirubin
Unconjugated (pre-hepatic — haemolysis, Gilbert’s) vs conjugated (hepatic / post-hepatic obstruction).
🏭Albumin & PT/INR
Synthetic function. A low albumin (chronic) or prolonged PT/INR (acute or severe) signals failing synthesis.
Typical adult ranges (check local lab): bilirubin <21 µmol/L · ALT <40 U/L · ALP 30–130 U/L · GGT <60 U/L · albumin 35–50 g/L.
2Hepatocellular vs cholestatic
↑↑ ALT/AST > ALP (hepatocellular)→Viral hepatitis, alcohol, drugs (paracetamol), NAFLD, autoimmune, ischaemic. Hepatitis / ALF ›
↑↑ ALP/GGT > ALT (cholestatic)→Obstruction (stones, tumour), PBC, PSC, drugs. Cholangitis ›
Low albumin / prolonged INR→Impaired synthesis — chronic liver disease or severe acute injury. Cirrhosis ›
3Bilirubin & jaundice
  • Unconjugated (pre-hepatic) — haemolysis or Gilbert’s; no bilirubinuria.
  • Conjugated — hepatic or post-hepatic; obstructive gives dark urine and pale stools.
  • An isolated raised bilirubin with otherwise normal LFTs, worse when fasting/unwell → Gilbert’s syndrome (benign).
🚩
Acute liver failure — jaundice with coagulopathy (INR ≥1.5) and encephalopathy — is an emergency: discuss early with a liver unit. Paracetamol overdose is the commonest UK cause — give N-acetylcysteine. Acute liver failure ›
📷 Image placeholder — an LFT pattern grid (hepatocellular vs cholestatic vs synthetic) mapped to the common causes, with the bilirubin metabolism pathway.
🎓 Exam pearl. ALT/AST = hepatocellular; ALP/GGT = cholestatic. A raised GGT confirms a hepatic ALP (vs bone). AST:ALT >2 → alcohol. Albumin + PT/INR = synthetic function. Acute liver failure = jaundice + coagulopathy + encephalopathy.
Amylase and lipase are pancreatic enzymes used to diagnose acute pancreatitis. Lipase is more sensitive and specific and stays raised longer — the preferred test where available.
1The two enzymes
⏱️Amylase
Rises early, falls within 24–48 h; >3× upper limit supports pancreatitis. Non-specific (raised in other abdominal pathology).
🎯Lipase
More sensitive & specific; stays elevated longer — better for late presentations. Preferred first-line where available.
2Diagnosing acute pancreatitis (2 of 3)
1. Characteristic epigastric pain → back2. Amylase/lipase >3× upper limit3. Characteristic CT imaging
Any two of three establish the diagnosis. Acute pancreatitis ›
3Caveats
  • Amylase can be normal in a late presentation, or in alcoholic / hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis — use lipase.
  • Non-pancreatic causes of a raised amylase: bowel perforation/ischaemia, ectopic pregnancy, DKA, parotitis, macroamylasaemia, renal failure.
  • The height of the amylase does NOT correlate with severity.
4Severity & cause
  • Score severity with Glasgow / APACHE II and CRP — not the enzyme level.
  • Find the cause — gallstones and alcohol are commonest (GET SMASHED). Chronic pancreatitis ›
  • Arrange an early abdominal ultrasound in every case to look for gallstones (the commonest cause).
🚩
Severe acute pancreatitis can cause organ failure (SIRS, ARDS, AKI). Assess severity with a validated score and CRP — never gauge it by the amylase level — and watch for complications (necrosis, pseudocyst).
🎓 Exam pearl. Lipase > amylase (more sensitive/specific, longer-lasting). >3× ULN is one of the 2-of-3 diagnostic criteria. The amylase level does not reflect severity — use Glasgow/CRP. Commonest causes: gallstones and ethanol.
Ammonia is a nitrogenous product of protein metabolism, detoxified by the liver via the urea cycle. It crosses the blood–brain barrier and is neurotoxic — measured mainly in hepatic encephalopathy and in unexplained encephalopathy.
1When to measure it
  • Hepatic encephalopathy — in cirrhosis or acute liver failure.
  • Unexplained encephalopathy/coma, especially in neonates/children → urea cycle disorders, organic acidaemias.
  • Valproate toxicity — hyperammonaemic encephalopathy without liver failure.
2Interpretation caveats
  • Sample handling matters — send on ice and analyse quickly; delay, haemolysis or a tourniquet falsely raise it.
  • The level correlates poorly with the grade of hepatic encephalopathy — it is supportive, not diagnostic. HE is a clinical diagnosis.
  • In established cirrhosis a routine ammonia is not required to diagnose HE — it is most useful when the cause of encephalopathy is unclear or to detect non-hepatic hyperammonaemia.
3Hepatic encephalopathy — management
  • Treat precipitants — infection, GI bleed, constipation, electrolyte disturbance, sedatives, dehydration.
  • Lactulose (lowers gut ammonia production/absorption) ± rifaximin. Cirrhosis ›
🚩
A very high ammonia in acute liver failure predicts cerebral oedema / raised ICP — an emergency needing urgent liver-unit (or metabolic) input. In a child with unexplained coma, a raised ammonia points to an inborn error of metabolism. Acute liver failure ›
🎓 Exam pearl. Ammonia is handled by the liver’s urea cycle; it rises in hepatic encephalopathy, urea cycle disorders and with valproate. It correlates poorly with HE grade (a clinical diagnosis) — send it on ice, run it fast. Treat precipitants + lactulose.
α₁-antitrypsin (A1AT) is a liver-made antiprotease that inhibits neutrophil elastase, protecting tissues — especially the lung. Deficiency causes early emphysema and liver disease.
1Deficiency — two organs
🫁Lung
Early-onset, basal-predominant emphysema (unopposed elastase) — especially in smokers and the young. COPD ›
🟡Liver
Neonatal jaundice/hepatitis, and childhood/adult cirrhosis and HCC — from misfolded protein accumulating in hepatocytes (PiZZ). Cirrhosis ›
2Testing
  • Measure the serum A1AT level (low) — but it is an acute-phase reactant, so a ‘normal’ level during inflammation can be misleading (check with CRP).
  • Confirm with phenotype/genotype (Pi typing): PiMM normal, PiZZ severe deficiency, PiMZ carrier.
3Management
  • Smoking cessation is critical (dramatically accelerates lung disease); manage COPD conventionally.
  • Monitor the liver; augmentation therapy in selected patients; family screening (heritable).
  • Liver transplantation is curative for the hepatic disease — it removes the source of the misfolded protein.
🚩
Consider A1AT deficiency in emphysema in a young or non-smoking patient, basal-predominant emphysema, or unexplained liver disease — a heritable diagnosis that is easily missed and has family implications.
🎓 Exam pearl. A1AT is an antiprotease protecting the lung from elastase. Deficiency → early basal emphysema (worse in smokers) + liver disease (PiZZ — misfolded protein accumulates in the liver). It is an acute-phase reactant, so confirm with Pi typing. Stop smoking.
Wilson’s disease is an autosomal-recessive disorder of copper metabolism (ATP7B) causing copper accumulation in the liver, brain and eyes. It is worked up with caeruloplasmin, 24-hour urinary copper and a slit-lamp exam.
1The copper picture
🔻Caeruloplasmin — LOW
The copper-carrying protein is low. Caveat: it is an acute-phase reactant, so it can be falsely normal in inflammation/pregnancy/oestrogens.
🔺24h urinary copper — HIGH
Excess free copper is excreted in the urine — a key diagnostic test (rises further after a penicillamine challenge).
🩸Serum copper
Total serum copper is often low (less caeruloplasmin), but the free (non-caeruloplasmin) copper is high — the toxic fraction.
👁️Kayser–Fleischer rings
Copper in Descemet’s membrane, seen on slit-lamp — especially with neurological disease.
2Who to test
  • A young patient (<40) with unexplained liver disease — hepatitis, cirrhosis or acute liver failure. Cirrhosis ›
  • Neuropsychiatric features — tremor, dysarthria, dystonia/parkinsonism, personality or psychiatric change.
3Confirming the diagnosis
  • A combination: low caeruloplasmin + high 24-h urinary copper + KF rings.
  • If uncertain: liver biopsy copper quantification and ATP7B genetic testing. Wilson’s disease ›
4Management
  • Copper chelation — penicillamine or trientine; zinc blocks gut absorption. Lifelong; avoid high-copper foods (liver, shellfish, nuts, chocolate).
  • Liver transplantation for fulminant or advanced disease (it corrects the metabolic defect).
  • Screen first-degree relatives (autosomal recessive) — presymptomatic treatment prevents disease.
🚩
Wilson’s presenting as acute liver failure is rapidly fatal without transplant → urgent liver unit. Classic clues: a low ALP, a Coombs-negative haemolytic anaemia, and a high bilirubin (a low ALP:bilirubin ratio). Acute liver failure ›
📷 Image placeholder — a slit-lamp photograph of Kayser–Fleischer rings (golden-brown ring at the corneal margin) and the copper-handling schematic.
🎓 Exam pearl. Wilson’s = low caeruloplasmin, high 24-h urinary copper, KF rings. Suspect it in a young patient with liver disease plus neuropsychiatric signs. Caeruloplasmin is an acute-phase reactant (can be normal). Treat with chelation (penicillamine/trientine) + zinc. The ALF form shows a low ALP and Coombs-negative haemolysis.
BIOCHEMISTRY__Bone & Calcium:
The bone profile — calcium, phosphate, ALP and albumin — is the first-line panel for calcium disorders, metabolic bone disease and monitoring. The single most important rule: always correct the calcium for albumin before interpreting it.
1What it measures
🦴Calcium (Ca²⁺)
Total calcium — about half is bound to albumin. The ionised fraction is physiologically active; report the albumin-corrected value.
🧪Phosphate (PO₄)
Regulated by PTH (lowers it), vitamin D and FGF23. Often moves opposite to calcium in PTH-driven disorders.
📈ALP
Alkaline phosphatase — raised with osteoblast activity (bone formation/turnover) and in cholestasis (liver). Also physiologically high in growth and pregnancy.
🧬Albumin
Needed to interpret the calcium — a low albumin lowers the total calcium without changing the ionised level.
2Corrected calcium
Corrected Ca (mmol/L) = measured Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin g/L)
A low albumin lowers the total calcium and can mask true hypercalcaemia (or falsely suggest hypocalcaemia). Correcting to an albumin of 40 g/L avoids this. Where accuracy is critical (e.g. critical illness), measure ionised calcium directly.
3Typical adult ranges (check local lab)
Adjusted Ca 2.20–2.60 mmol/LPhosphate 0.8–1.5 mmol/LALP 30–130 U/LAlbumin 35–50 g/L
4Read the profile
↑ Corrected calcium→Mostly primary hyperparathyroidism (outpatient) or malignancy (inpatient). Hypercalcaemia ›
↓ Corrected calcium→Vitamin D deficiency, CKD, hypoparathyroidism. Hypocalcaemia ›
Isolated ↑ ALP→Check the GGT: raised → hepatic/cholestatic; normal → bony (Paget’s, osteomalacia, mets, healing fracture). Metabolic bone disease ›
🚩
Severe hypercalcaemia (corrected Ca >3.0 mmol/L) or a symptomatic patient (confusion, dehydration, arrhythmia) is an emergency → IV 0.9% saline rehydration, then an IV bisphosphonate (e.g. zoledronate) for hypercalcaemia of malignancy; treat the underlying cause (malignancy or primary hyperparathyroidism). Severe hypocalcaemia can cause tetany, seizures and a prolonged QT.
📷 Image placeholder — a bone-profile interpretation grid: calcium (corrected), phosphate, ALP and PTH across the common patterns (primary/secondary hyperparathyroidism, osteomalacia, Paget’s, CKD-MBD).
🎓 Exam pearl. Always correct the calcium for albumin. A raised ALP is bone vs liver — the GGT splits them (raised = hepatic, normal = bony). Interpret calcium with phosphate and PTH together (see the PTH tab).
A calcium disorder is worked up by measuring PTH and vitamin D alongside the corrected calcium. The trick is to read the PTH relative to the calcium — is it appropriately suppressed/raised, or inappropriate?
1The hormones
🧫PTH
Raises calcium (bone resorption, renal Ca reabsorption, activates vitamin D) and lowers phosphate. Interpret it relative to the calcium.
☀️Vitamin D (25-OH)
The storage form measured; activated to 1,25-(OH)₂ in the kidney. Increases gut absorption of calcium and phosphate. Low → deficiency.
2The calcium + PTH grid
⬆️↑ Ca · ↑ / normal PTH
Primary hyperparathyroidism (PTH inappropriately non-suppressed). Also tertiary hyperPTH and FHH. Hyperparathyroidism ›
⬆️↑ Ca · ↓ PTH
Malignancy (PTHrP or bone mets) — the PTH is appropriately suppressed. Also vitamin D excess and sarcoidosis ›.
⬇️↓ Ca · ↑ PTH
Secondary hyperparathyroidism — an appropriate response to vitamin D deficiency or CKD ›.
⬇️↓ Ca · ↓ / normal PTH
Hypoparathyroidism (post-surgical, autoimmune) — PTH inappropriately low. Also severe hypomagnesaemia. Hypoparathyroidism ›
Phosphate adds a clue: it is low where PTH/PTHrP action dominates (primary hyperPTH, malignancy) or in vitamin D deficiency, but high in hypoparathyroidism and CKD (impaired excretion).
3Vitamin D & two classic traps
  • Low 25-OH vitamin D → deficiency → secondary hyperPTH and osteomalacia / rickets (metabolic bone disease ›). The active 1,25 form is raised in sarcoidosis and other granulomatous disease (a cause of hypercalcaemia).
  • FHH (familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia) mimics primary hyperPTH (↑Ca, ↑/normal PTH) but has a LOW urine calcium — check the calcium:creatinine clearance ratio before referring for surgery.
  • Magnesium — severe hypomagnesaemia causes functional hypoparathyroidism: hypocalcaemia that is refractory until the magnesium is replaced.
🚩
Symptomatic hypocalcaemia — tetany, carpopedal spasm, seizures, a prolonged QT (Chvostek’s / Trousseau’s signs) — needs IV calcium gluconate with cardiac monitoring. Always check magnesium, as hypocalcaemia will not correct while it is low.
📷 Image placeholder — the calcium/PTH 2×2 quadrant with worked bloods in each box, plus the vitamin D → PTH → calcium regulatory axis.
🎓 Exam pearl. Read PTH against the calcium: ↑Ca + ↑PTH = primary hyperparathyroidism; ↑Ca + ↓PTH = malignancy; ↓Ca + ↑PTH = secondary (vit D deficiency / CKD); ↓Ca + ↓PTH = hypoparathyroidism. FHH mimics primary hyperPTH — check urine calcium. Correct magnesium in refractory hypocalcaemia.
The bone profile fingerprints the metabolic bone diseases. The single highest-yield fact: osteoporosis is biochemically NORMAL — it is diagnosed on DEXA, not on bloods — whereas osteomalacia, Paget’s and renal bone disease each have a signature.
1The pattern grid (Ca · PO₄ · ALP · PTH)
🦴Osteoporosis
ALL NORMAL (Ca, PO₄, ALP, PTH). Diagnosis is on DEXA (T-score ≤ −2.5), not the bone profile. Metabolic bone disease ›
☀️Osteomalacia / rickets
↓Ca · ↓PO₄ · ↑ALP · ↑PTH with a low vitamin D — the secondary-hyperparathyroidism picture of vitamin D deficiency. Look for proximal myopathy and Looser’s zones (pseudofractures) on X-ray.
📈Paget’s disease
Isolated ↑↑ALP with normal Ca and PO₄. High bone turnover → bone pain, deformity, deafness.
⬆️Primary hyperparathyroidism
↑Ca · ↓PO₄ · ↑PTH (± ↑ALP if bone disease). Hyperparathyroidism ›
🫘CKD-MBD (renal)
↓Ca · ↑PO₄ · ↑ALP · ↑↑PTH — the exception where phosphate is high (impaired excretion). CKD ›
2Osteoporosis — a normal profile
  • Diagnosed on DEXA: T-score ≤ −2.5 = osteoporosis; −1 to −2.5 = osteopenia. Fracture risk is estimated with FRAX / QFracture.
  • The bone profile is checked mainly to exclude secondary causes — myeloma, osteomalacia, hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism.
  • First-line treatment is a bisphosphonate (e.g. alendronate) with adequate calcium and vitamin D.
3Paget’s disease
  • Isolated, often very high ALP with normal calcium. Bone pain, bowing of long bones, skull enlargement, deafness.
  • Confirm with X-ray and an isotope bone scan; treat symptomatic disease with a bisphosphonate.
🚩
New bone pain with hypercalcaemia, anaemia or renal impairment → exclude myeloma. A key discriminator: myeloma classically has a NORMAL ALP despite lytic lesions (osteoclast-driven, no osteoblastic response) — unlike bone metastases or Paget’s. Myeloma ›
📷 Image placeholder — the metabolic-bone-disease table (Ca / PO₄ / ALP / PTH across osteoporosis, osteomalacia, Paget’s, primary hyperPTH, CKD-MBD) alongside classic X-rays.
🎓 Exam pearl. Osteoporosis = normal bone profile (DEXA diagnoses it). Osteomalacia = ↓Ca ↓PO₄ ↑ALP ↑PTH + low vitamin D. Paget’s = isolated ↑↑ALP, normal Ca. CKD = ↓Ca ↑PO₄ ↑ALP ↑↑PTH. Myeloma = normal ALP despite lytic lesions.
BIOCHEMISTRY__Diabetes & Glucose:
Diabetes is diagnosed and monitored with glucose and HbA1c. HbA1c (glycated haemoglobin) reflects average glycaemia over ~3 months and needs no fasting.
1The tests
🩸HbA1c
Glycated haemoglobin — ~8–12 week average (red-cell lifespan). ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%) = diabetes. No fasting needed.
⏱️Fasting glucose
≥7.0 mmol/L = diabetes (fasted ≥8 h).
🍬Random / 2h OGTT
≥11.1 mmol/L = diabetes (random with symptoms, or 2-h value on a 75 g OGTT).
2Diagnosis
  • Symptomatic (osmotic symptoms) + one abnormal result → diabetes.
  • Asymptomatic → needs two abnormal results (repeat to confirm).
  • Prediabetes: HbA1c 42–47, impaired fasting glucose 6.1–6.9, or impaired glucose tolerance (2-h 7.8–11.0). Type 2 diabetes ›
  • Prediabetes → intensive lifestyle intervention and annual review (high risk of progression).
3Monitoring
  • HbA1c every 3–6 months; individualised targets (~48–58 mmol/mol).
  • Capillary glucose / CGM for day-to-day control.
🚩
Very high glucose with ketones and acidosis → DKA; very high glucose with marked dehydration but no ketosis → HHS. Both are emergencies. Diabetic emergencies ›
📷 Image placeholder — a diagnostic-thresholds table (HbA1c / fasting / 2h OGTT) with the diabetes vs prediabetes cut-offs.
🎓 Exam pearl. Diabetes: HbA1c ≥48 (6.5%), fasting ≥7.0, 2-h/random ≥11.1. HbA1c = a 3-month average, no fasting. If asymptomatic, confirm with a second abnormal test.
The HbA1c thresholds are precise, but the test is unreliable whenever red-cell turnover is abnormal — know when not to use it.
1Thresholds
Diabetes ≥48 mmol/mol (6.5%)High risk / prediabetes 42–47Normal <42
Asymptomatic → repeat to confirm; symptomatic → one result suffices.
2When HbA1c is unreliable
🔻Falsely LOW
Reduced RBC lifespan / high turnover: haemolysis, recent blood loss or transfusion, pregnancy, reticulocytosis, splenomegaly, and CKD/dialysis (reduced red-cell survival).
🔺Falsely HIGH
Increased RBC lifespan: untreated iron/B12/folate deficiency anaemia, splenectomy.
🚫Not valid at all
Rapid-onset diabetes (suspected type 1, children), acute illness, pancreatic damage, steroids, and haemoglobinopathies (HbS/HbC interfere).
3What to use instead
  • Use fasting glucose or an OGTT for diagnosis when HbA1c is invalid.
  • Fructosamine (glycated albumin) reflects ~2–3 weeks and is an alternative for monitoring.
🚩
Do not use HbA1c to diagnose diabetes in pregnancy, suspected type 1 (rapid onset/ketosis), or with anaemia/haemoglobinopathy — use glucose-based criteria instead. Type 1 diabetes ›
🎓 Exam pearl. HbA1c ≥48 = diabetes (confirm if asymptomatic). It is unreliable with abnormal RBC turnover: iron deficiency raises it; haemolysis/pregnancy lower it. Use glucose/OGTT instead; fructosamine for short-term monitoring.
When the type of diabetes is unclear, use C-peptide (a marker of endogenous insulin) and diabetes autoantibodies (GAD, IA-2) to classify — and to work up hypoglycaemia.
1C-peptide
  • Co-secreted 1:1 with insulin from beta cells → a marker of endogenous insulin production.
  • Low/undetectable → type 1 (beta-cell failure). Preserved/high → type 2 or MODY. Type 1 › / Type 2 ›
  • Interpret C-peptide with a paired glucose — a low C-peptide is only meaningful when glucose is not low.
2Diabetes autoantibodies
  • GAD (anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase), IA-2, ZnT8, islet-cell antibodies.
  • Positive → autoimmune type 1 (or LADA — latent autoimmune diabetes in adults).
3When to test
Adult ‘type 2’ behaving atypically→Lean, ketosis-prone, poor response → check antibodies/C-peptide for LADA / type 1.
Young + strong family history→Antibody-negative with preserved C-peptide → consider MODY (genetic testing).
4Hypoglycaemia work-up
High insulin + HIGH C-peptide→Endogenous — insulinoma or a sulfonylurea (send a drug screen).
High insulin + LOW C-peptide→Exogenous insulin administration.
🚩
If a patient is ketosis-prone or rapidly deteriorating, treat as type 1 with insulin now — do not withhold insulin while awaiting antibody/C-peptide results. Diabetic emergencies ›
🎓 Exam pearl. C-peptide = endogenous insulin (low in type 1, preserved in type 2/MODY). GAD/IA-2 positive = autoimmune (type 1/LADA). Antibody-negative + preserved C-peptide + family history = MODY. Hypo: high insulin with high C-peptide = insulinoma/sulfonylurea, low C-peptide = exogenous insulin.
BIOCHEMISTRY__Cardiac Markers:
Cardiac troponin (cTnI/cTnT) is the biomarker of myocardial injury — highly sensitive and specific and now the standard test; CK/CK-MB are older markers. A troponin rise means myocardial injury, which is not always myocardial infarction.
1The markers
❤️Troponin (cTn)
Released from damaged myocardium — rises 3–6 h, peaks 12–24 h, stays up for days. High-sensitivity assays detect tiny early rises. The preferred test.
💪CK / CK-MB
Less specific (also skeletal muscle); CK-MB is more cardiac. Largely superseded, but CK-MB falls faster so it can help detect re-infarction.
2Injury vs infarction
MI (4th Universal Definition) = a rise and/or fall of troponin with at least one value >99th percentile, PLUS evidence of ischaemia (symptoms, ischaemic ECG changes, or imaging).
A raised troponin without that ischaemic context is injury, not MI. Within an MI, type 1 is atherothrombotic (plaque rupture) and type 2 is a supply–demand mismatch. Acute coronary syndrome ›
3Non-ACS causes of a raised troponin
Type 2 MI (supply-demand: sepsis, tachyarrhythmia, anaemia, hypotension)PEHeart failureMyocarditisCKD (reduced clearance)Post-cardiac-arrestAortic dissection
4How to interpret
  • Look for a dynamic rise/fall on serial troponins, in the right clinical context.
  • A single raised troponin that is static, without ischaemia, is often chronic (CKD, structural heart disease).
🚩
STEMI is diagnosed on the ECG — arrange immediate reperfusion (PCI); do not wait for troponin. Chest pain + a troponin rise + ischaemic ECG → treat as ACS. ACS ›
📷 Image placeholder — cardiac biomarker release curves (troponin vs CK-MB vs myoglobin over time post-MI).
🎓 Exam pearl. Troponin = myocardial injury (sensitive/specific), not always MI. MI needs a rise/fall + ischaemia evidence. Many non-ACS causes (type 2 MI, PE, HF, myocarditis, CKD). STEMI is treated on the ECG — don’t wait for troponin.
High-sensitivity troponin rule-in/rule-out pathways use paired troponins (0 and 1 h, or 0 and 3 h) with assay-specific thresholds to triage chest pain rapidly — always alongside the ECG and clinical risk.
1The 0/1-hour algorithm (ESC)
✅Rule OUT
A very low baseline, or a low baseline with no significant 1-h change (delta) → MI ruled out (high negative predictive value).
⛔Rule IN
A high baseline or a significant 1-h rise (delta) → MI ruled in → treat as ACS.
🔁Observe
The in-between zone → repeat at 3 h, reconsider other diagnoses, and consider further imaging.
2Key principles
  • The delta (change) matters as much as the absolute value — a dynamic rise/fall points to acute injury.
  • Thresholds are assay-specific (hs-cTnT ≠ cTnI) and the 99th percentile is sex-specific.
  • Interpret with a risk score (HEART) and the ECG — never in isolation.
  • With hs-troponin, unstable angina has a normal troponin (ischaemic symptoms, no rise); a troponin rise/fall reclassifies it as NSTEMI.
3Pitfalls
  • Very early presentation (<1–2 h from pain onset) — a single low troponin may miss it; repeat.
  • Chronically elevated troponin (CKD, structural heart disease) — rely on the delta, not the absolute value.
🚩
A rapid rule-out only applies with a low-risk clinical assessment and a non-ischaemic ECG. Never rule out on troponin alone with ongoing pain or high risk — and a STEMI is treated on the ECG, not the troponin. ACS ›
🎓 Exam pearl. hs-troponin pathways (0/1 h or 0/3 h) rule MI in/out using the baseline + delta. Interpret with the ECG and a risk score (HEART). Thresholds are assay- and sex-specific. Don’t rule out with ongoing pain, high risk, or an ischaemic ECG.
BNP and NT-proBNP are released from ventricular myocardium in response to wall stretch/stress. Their main value in suspected heart failure is as a rule-out test — a normal level makes HF unlikely (high negative predictive value).
1What it is
  • Released when the ventricles are stretched (volume/pressure overload). NT-proBNP is the inactive fragment — longer half-life and more stable.
  • A normal level in an untreated patient effectively excludes heart failure; higher levels track severity/prognosis.
2Suspected heart failure (NICE, NT-proBNP)
✅< 400 ng/L
Heart failure unlikely — consider other causes.
📅400–2000 ng/L
Refer for echocardiography within 6 weeks.
🚨> 2000 ng/L
Urgent referral + echo within 2 weeks (a high level carries a worse prognosis).
A raised level → echocardiography to confirm and characterise. Chronic heart failure › (These are the chronic-pathway thresholds; in acute breathlessness an NT-proBNP <300 ng/L makes acute HF unlikely.)
3Other influences on the level
Raised (not just HF)→Older age, AF, renal impairment (reduced clearance), PE, sepsis, LVH, valve disease.
Falsely low→Obesity lowers BNP.
On sacubitril/valsartan (ARNI)→Neprilysin inhibition raises BNP — monitor with NT-proBNP instead.
🚩
Acute breathlessness with a very high BNP/NT-proBNP suggests acute heart failure → urgent assessment and echo — but a raised level is non-specific, so also consider PE and sepsis. Acute heart failure ›
🎓 Exam pearl. BNP/NT-proBNP = ventricular stretch marker; best as a rule-OUT for HF (high NPV). Raised → echo. Also raised by age, AF, CKD, PE; lower in obesity. Sacubitril raises BNP → monitor with NT-proBNP.
The lipid profile — total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides and non-HDL — assesses cardiovascular risk and guides lipid-lowering therapy. Fasting is not needed for most samples.
1The components
Total cholesterolLDL (atherogenic)HDL (protective)TriglyceridesNon-HDL = total − HDL
Non-HDL cholesterol is the modern treatment target (captures all atherogenic particles; no fasting required).
2Primary prevention
  • QRISK3 ≥10% (10-year CV risk) → offer atorvastatin 20 mg. Lipid disorders ›
  • Also treat those with type 1 diabetes (per criteria) and CKD.
3Secondary prevention & targets
  • Established CVD → atorvastatin 80 mg (high-intensity).
  • Aim for a ≥40% reduction in non-HDL cholesterol; recheck at 3 months (add ezetimibe ± a PCSK9 inhibitor if not met).
  • Before a statin: exclude secondary causes (e.g. hypothyroidism), check baseline LFTs; statins can cause myopathy — check CK if muscle symptoms.
4Two things not to miss
Familial hypercholesterolaemia→Very high LDL/total cholesterol, tendon xanthomata, family history of premature CVD → specialist + cascade screening.
Very high triglycerides (>10 mmol/L)→Risk of acute pancreatitis → fibrate + lifestyle; look for secondary causes (alcohol, diabetes, hypothyroidism). Pancreatitis ›
🚩
Familial hypercholesterolaemia is under-diagnosed — suspect it with a very high cholesterol, tendon xanthomata or a family history of early heart disease, and arrange cascade screening of relatives. Triglycerides >10 mmol/L risk acute pancreatitis.
🎓 Exam pearl. Non-HDL cholesterol is the modern target (no fasting). QRISK ≥10% → atorvastatin 20; established CVD → atorvastatin 80; aim ≥40% non-HDL reduction. FH: high LDL + tendon xanthomata + early-CVD family history → cascade screen. Very high TG → pancreatitis.
BIOCHEMISTRY__Endocrine:
Thyroid function tests = TSH + free T4 (± free T3). TSH is the most sensitive first-line test — interpret it together with the free T4.
1Read the pattern (TSH + fT4)
↓ TSH · ↑ fT4→Primary hyperthyroidism (Graves’, toxic nodule). Hyperthyroidism ›
↑ TSH · ↓ fT4→Primary hypothyroidism (Hashimoto’s). Hypothyroidism ›
↑ TSH · normal fT4→Subclinical hypothyroidism.
↓ TSH · normal fT4→Subclinical hyperthyroidism (check fT3 for T3 toxicosis).
Low fT4 · low/normal TSH→Central (secondary) hypothyroidism or sick euthyroid.
Typical ranges (check local lab): TSH 0.4–4.0 mU/L · free T4 9–25 pmol/L · free T3 3.5–6.5 pmol/L.
2Antibodies & further tests
  • TPO antibodies — Hashimoto’s and Graves’. TSH-receptor antibodies (TRAb) — Graves’.
  • Free T3 for suspected T3 toxicosis; isotope uptake scan to find the cause of thyrotoxicosis.
3Caveats
  • Sick euthyroid (non-thyroidal illness) — TFTs are often abnormal during acute illness; don’t test then, repeat once recovered.
  • Interference: biotin, amiodarone, lithium, steroids (lower TSH); pregnancy needs trimester-specific ranges.
  • Central hypothyroidism — the TSH may be low/normal despite a low T4, so do not rely on TSH alone.
🚩
Thyroid storm (severe thyrotoxicosis: fever, tachyarrhythmia, agitation/delirium) and myxoedema coma (severe hypothyroidism: hypothermia, reduced GCS) are medical emergencies.
📷 Image placeholder — a TSH/fT4 interpretation grid mapping the hyper/hypo/subclinical/central patterns.
🎓 Exam pearl. TSH is the most sensitive first-line test. ↓TSH+↑T4 = hyperthyroid; ↑TSH+↓T4 = hypothyroid; ↑TSH+normal T4 = subclinical hypothyroid. Don’t test in acute illness (sick euthyroid). Central hypothyroidism → low T4 with inappropriately normal/low TSH.
Screen for secondary (endocrine) hypertension in the young, resistant, or severe/accelerated hypertensive, or with suggestive features. The key tests: aldosterone:renin ratio (Conn’s), metanephrines (phaeo) and cortisol (Cushing’s).
1Who to screen
Young (<40)Resistant (≥3 drugs)Severe / acceleratedHypokalaemiaSuggestive symptoms/signs
2The three endocrine screens
🧂Aldosterone:renin ratio
Raised ARR → primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn’s): hypertension ± hypokalaemia (often normokalaemic) + alkalosis. Conn’s ›
💥Metanephrines
Plasma/urine metanephrines → phaeochromocytoma: episodic headache, sweating, palpitations, paroxysmal HTN. Phaeochromocytoma ›
🌙Cortisol
Overnight dexamethasone suppression / late-night salivary / 24h urinary cortisol → Cushing’s: central obesity, striae, bruising, proximal myopathy. Cushing’s ›
3Other secondary causes
Renal artery stenosisCKDThyroid diseaseCoarctationDrugs (OCP, steroids, NSAIDs, sympathomimetics)OSA
4Interpretation caveats
  • Many drugs distort the ARR (spironolactone, beta-blockers, ACEi/ARB) — washout and careful interpretation are needed.
  • A positive screen is followed by a confirmatory test and imaging.
🚩
In phaeochromocytoma, never start a beta-blocker before alpha-blockade — unopposed alpha-stimulation can precipitate a hypertensive crisis. Suspect it with paroxysmal headache, sweating and palpitations. Phaeochromocytoma ›
🎓 Exam pearl. Screen secondary HTN if young / resistant / severe. Conn’s → ARR (HTN + low K⁺); phaeo → metanephrines; Cushing’s → dexamethasone suppression / cortisol. In phaeo, alpha-block before beta-block.
IGF-1 is the screening test for acromegaly (growth-hormone excess). Because GH is pulsatile, it is measured indirectly via the stable, GH-driven IGF-1; diagnosis is confirmed with an OGTT.
1Why IGF-1, not a random GH?
  • GH is pulsatile (varies widely through the day) — a random GH is unreliable.
  • IGF-1 (made by the liver in response to GH) is stable and integrates GH over time → the screening test (age/sex-adjusted).
2Confirming the diagnosis
  • OGTT with GH measurement: glucose normally suppresses GH; in acromegaly GH fails to suppress (paradoxical) — the confirmatory test.
  • Then a pituitary MRI to identify the adenoma. Acromegaly ›
3Who to test (clinical clues)
Acral enlargement (hands, feet)Jaw prognathism, coarse featuresSweating, headachesBitemporal hemianopiaCarpal tunnelDiabetes, hypertension, OSA, colon polyps
4Management
  • Trans-sphenoidal surgery (first-line); medical options — somatostatin analogues (octreotide), pegvisomant, cabergoline.
  • Monitor with IGF-1 (and OGTT-GH).
  • Surveillance: colonoscopy (increased colon-cancer risk), assess the other pituitary axes and formal visual fields.
🚩
Untreated acromegaly increases cardiovascular and colorectal-cancer mortality. A pituitary macroadenoma can compress the optic chiasm → bitemporal hemianopia, needing urgent assessment.
🎓 Exam pearl. IGF-1 = screening test for acromegaly (GH is pulsatile). Confirm with an OGTT — GH fails to suppress. Then pituitary MRI. Features: acral/jaw growth, bitemporal hemianopia, diabetes/HTN/colon cancer. IGF-1 is physiologically high in puberty and pregnancy.
Serum ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) is produced by granulomas. In sarcoidosis it is a supportive, non-diagnostic marker — used mainly to monitor disease activity, not to diagnose or exclude.
1What it is
  • Made by the epithelioid cells of granulomas. Raised in ~60% of sarcoidosis — so a normal level does not exclude it.
  • Non-specific — also raised in other granulomatous/other disease: TB, leprosy, histoplasmosis, hyperthyroidism, diabetes, silicosis.
2Use & limitations
  • Not diagnostic (limited sensitivity and specificity). Diagnosis of sarcoidosis is clinical + radiological + histological (non-caseating granulomas).
  • Main value: trending disease activity and treatment response in known sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis ›
3The rest of the work-up
CXR — bilateral hilar lymphadenopathySerum calcium (hypercalcaemia)CRP / ESRBiopsy — non-caseating granulomasLöfgren’s: EN + BHL + arthralgia (good prognosis)
4Caveats
  • ACE inhibitors lower the serum ACE (drug interference).
  • Genetic ACE polymorphisms affect the baseline level between individuals.
🚩
Sarcoid hypercalcaemia (macrophage 1,25-vitamin D production; hypercalciuria is even more common) can cause renal impairment and stones; cardiac and neurosarcoidosis are serious. Serum ACE is not used to diagnose or exclude sarcoidosis. Sarcoidosis ›
🎓 Exam pearl. Serum ACE = granuloma marker; supportive, not diagnostic in sarcoidosis (raised in ~60%, non-specific). Diagnosis = clinical + imaging + biopsy (non-caseating granulomas). Watch for hypercalcaemia (1,25-vitamin D). ACE inhibitors lower the level.
BIOCHEMISTRY__Tumour Markers:
Tumour markers are mainly for monitoring and follow-up of a known cancer — not for screening or diagnosis. CA19-9 (pancreatobiliary) and CEA (colorectal) are the classic examples.
1The golden rule
Tumour markers lack the sensitivity and specificity to diagnose or screen. Their value is tracking treatment response and detecting recurrence in a patient with an established cancer.
2CA19-9
  • Raised in pancreatic and biliary (cholangiocarcinoma) cancers → monitoring and assessing recurrence. Pancreatic cancer › / Cholangiocarcinoma ›
  • Also raised (benign): obstructive jaundice / cholestasis, pancreatitis, cirrhosis — recheck after biliary drainage.
  • Falsely normal in Lewis-antigen-negative people (~5–10% don’t secrete CA19-9).
  • A very high CA19-9 in pancreatic cancer suggests advanced / unresectable disease (prognostic).
3CEA
  • Raised in colorectal cancer — used to monitor for recurrence after resection, not to screen or diagnose. Colorectal cancer ›
  • Non-specific: smoking, IBD, pancreatitis and other GI cancers also raise it. Bowel-cancer screening = FIT/colonoscopy, not CEA.
🚩
Do not use tumour markers to screen asymptomatic people or to diagnose cancer — false positives and negatives cause real harm. A rising trend after treatment suggests recurrence → confirm with imaging. Remember obstructive jaundice raises CA19-9.
📷 Image placeholder — a tumour-marker → primary-cancer map (CA19-9 pancreatobiliary, CEA colorectal, AFP HCC/germ-cell, PSA prostate, hCG/AFP testicular).
🎓 Exam pearl. Tumour markers = monitoring / follow-up, not screening/diagnosis. CA19-9 → pancreatic/biliary (also raised in cholestasis; falsely normal in Lewis-negative). CEA → colorectal (recurrence). A rising trend = recurrence.
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is used in HCC surveillance (with ultrasound) in high-risk liver disease, and as a germ-cell tumour marker. As with all tumour markers, interpret the trend alongside imaging.
1AFP in liver disease
  • Raised in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). HCC ›
  • HCC surveillance: 6-monthly ultrasound ± AFP in cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B. AFP alone has limited sensitivity — ultrasound is the mainstay. Cirrhosis ›
2Other causes of a raised AFP
Non-seminomatous germ-cell (yolk-sac) tumoursPregnancy (physiological; also a fetal screening marker)Active hepatitis / liver regeneration (mild)
A raised AFP indicates a non-seminomatous element — pure seminoma does NOT raise AFP.
3Interpreting
  • A markedly raised or rising AFP in cirrhosis with a liver lesion → HCC — classic imaging (contrast CT/MRI) may be diagnostic without biopsy.
  • Modest rises are non-specific (active hepatitis) — rely on the trend + imaging.
🚩
A new liver lesion in a cirrhotic with a rising AFP is HCC until proven otherwise → urgent imaging and MDT referral. Structured surveillance in cirrhosis detects HCC early and saves lives. HCC ›
🎓 Exam pearl. AFP → HCC (surveillance with 6-monthly US in cirrhosis; US is the mainstay) and germ-cell (yolk-sac) tumours. Also raised in pregnancy and active hepatitis. A rising AFP + liver lesion in cirrhosis = HCC.
PSA (prostate-specific antigen) is made by the prostate — used to detect and monitor prostate cancer, but it is organ-specific, not cancer-specific. Refinements (density, free:total ratio, velocity) improve its specificity.
1What raises PSA (not just cancer)
Prostate cancerBPHProstatitis / UTIUrinary retention, catheterDRE, ejaculationVigorous exercise / cycling
Check PSA before a DRE, and defer after a recent UTI, ejaculation or catheterisation. BPH ›
2Refinements that favour cancer
📉Low free:total ratio
Cancer binds more PSA, so a LOW free:total favours malignancy; a high ratio favours BPH.
📐High PSA density
PSA ÷ prostate volume — a higher density favours cancer over simple BPH.
📈High PSA velocity
A rapid rise / short doubling time over serial tests favours cancer.
3Pathway
  • Use age-specific thresholds (NICE referral guide: roughly >3.0 at 50–59, >4.0 at 60–69, higher at ≥70). A raised PSA → refer (2-week wait) → mpMRI then targeted biopsy. Prostate cancer ›
  • Screening is controversial (no national programme) — a shared, informed decision.
  • Monitoring: after prostatectomy PSA should be undetectable; a rising PSA = recurrence.
🚩
A very high PSA with bone pain suggests metastatic prostate cancer (sclerotic bone mets). Back pain with neurology → metastatic spinal cord compression, an emergency (urgent MRI + dexamethasone). Prostate cancer ›
🎓 Exam pearl. PSA is non-specific (BPH, prostatitis, UTI, retention, DRE, ejaculation) — check before a DRE. Low free:total and high density/velocity favour cancer. Raised → mpMRI + biopsy. Rising PSA after treatment = recurrence.
Testicular germ-cell tumours are worked up with AFP, β-hCG and LDH — supporting diagnosis, and used for staging, prognosis and monitoring. Markers are taken before and after orchidectomy.
1The three markers
🧬AFP
Non-seminomatous (yolk-sac/embryonal). NOT raised in pure seminoma — a key discriminator.
🤰β-hCG
Trophoblastic — high in choriocarcinoma; mildly raised in ~15–20% of seminomas. A high level can cause gynaecomastia.
📊LDH
A marker of tumour bulk / turnover (non-specific) — used for staging and prognosis.
2Seminoma vs non-seminoma
A raised AFP means NON-seminomatous disease — even if the histology looks like seminoma, an elevated AFP means it is treated as a non-seminomatous germ-cell tumour (NSGCT).
Pure seminoma: AFP normal; β-hCG sometimes mildly raised; LDH may be raised.
3How they are used
  • Measured before and after orchidectomy; post-orchidectomy levels feed the S category of TNM staging (prognosis).
  • Half-life monitoring — AFP ~5–7 days, β-hCG ~24–36 h; failure to fall as expected suggests residual/metastatic disease.
🚩
A testicular mass is cancer until proven otherwise → urgent ultrasound + markers + urology referral. Do NOT biopsy the testis (risk of seeding) — perform a radical inguinal orchidectomy. Testicular cancer ›
🎓 Exam pearl. AFP = non-seminoma (NOT pure seminoma); β-hCG = choriocarcinoma / some seminomas; LDH = tumour bulk. A raised AFP → treat as NSGCT. Markers taken pre/post-orchidectomy for the S stage and monitoring (half-lives). Don’t biopsy — orchidectomy.
BIOCHEMISTRY__Sepsis, Metabolic & Screen:
CRP and procalcitonin are inflammatory markers that support the diagnosis of infection/sepsis and help guide antibiotics. Procalcitonin is more specific for bacterial infection — but neither diagnoses sepsis, which is a clinical call.
1The two markers
🔥CRP
Hepatic acute-phase protein — rises in infection, inflammation, tissue damage and malignancy. Sensitive but non-specific; rises 6–8 h, peaks ~48 h. Trend it to monitor response.
🦠Procalcitonin (PCT)
Rises more specifically with bacterial infection/sepsis (less with viral/inflammation); rises fast (2–4 h). Used in antibiotic stewardship (start/stop).
2How they help
  • CRP — supports diagnosis and, on serial testing, tracks response to treatment.
  • Procalcitonin — helps distinguish bacterial from viral and guides antibiotic duration (PCT-guided stopping safely reduces antibiotic use).
3Caveats
  • CRP is raised by many non-infective causes — surgery, MI, trauma, malignancy, autoimmune disease. A very high CRP (>100) suggests significant bacterial infection but is not specific.
  • A normal CRP does not exclude serious infection in the immunosuppressed or elderly (a blunted response).
  • PCT also rises with major surgery/trauma, burns and cardiogenic shock; renal impairment affects clearance.
🚩
Do not wait for CRP or procalcitonin to treat suspected sepsis. Sepsis is a clinical diagnosis — deliver the Sepsis 6 (cultures, lactate, antibiotics, IV fluids, urine output, oxygen) within 1 hour. Sepsis ›
📷 Image placeholder — CRP vs procalcitonin kinetics after the onset of bacterial infection, with the antibiotic-stewardship decision points.
🎓 Exam pearl. CRP = sensitive but non-specific acute-phase marker (trend to monitor). Procalcitonin = more specific for bacterial infection and guides antibiotic stewardship. Neither diagnoses sepsis — treat clinically with the Sepsis 6.
Lactate is a marker of tissue hypoperfusion / anaerobic metabolism — a key severity marker in sepsis and shock, and a target for resuscitation. >2 is abnormal; >4 mmol/L is severe.
1Type A vs Type B
🫀Type A (hypoxic)
Inadequate oxygen delivery: sepsis, shock (any), cardiac arrest, ischaemia (bowel/limb), severe hypoxia or anaemia.
💊Type B (non-hypoxic)
Not from hypoperfusion: liver failure (reduced clearance), metformin, DKA, thiamine deficiency, malignancy, seizures, salbutamol, alcohol.
2In sepsis & shock
  • Lactate is part of the Sepsis 6. A lactate >2 (especially >4) signals severity → aggressive fluid resuscitation. Sepsis › / Shock ›
  • Lactate clearance (a falling level with treatment) is a good prognostic sign; a persistent or rising lactate is ominous.
3Caveats
  • Venous lactate is fine for screening; arterial is more accurate. A tourniquet or delayed processing falsely raises it.
  • Metformin-associated lactic acidosis — especially with AKI (drug accumulation).
  • A raised lactate produces a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (see the ABG / acid–base tab).
🚩
A lactate >4 mmol/L in an unwell patient indicates tissue hypoperfusion / shock → resuscitate and escalate urgently. If unexplained, consider mesenteric or limb ischaemia. Shock ›
🎓 Exam pearl. Lactate = tissue hypoperfusion marker. >2 abnormal, >4 severe. Type A (hypoxia/shock — sepsis, ischaemia) vs Type B (metformin, liver failure, DKA, thiamine). Part of the Sepsis 6; lactate clearance = good prognosis.
Refeeding syndrome is a dangerous shift of electrolytes — above all phosphate — when feeding is reintroduced to a starved/malnourished patient. Monitor phosphate, potassium and magnesium.
1The mechanism
Starvation depletes intracellular stores. Re-introducing carbohydrate triggers an insulin surge → cells take up phosphate, potassium and magnesium → plasma levels fall sharply.
Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark → arrhythmia, cardiac/respiratory failure, rhabdomyolysis, seizures.
2Who is at risk (NICE)
Little/no intake >5 daysBMI <16Unintentional weight loss >15%Low baseline K/PO₄/MgAlcohol / drug misuseChemotherapy
Common in eating disorders and prolonged undernutrition. Eating disorders › / Nutrition ›
3Prevention & management
  • Check phosphate, potassium, magnesium (± glucose) before and daily during refeeding.
  • Start feeding slowly (e.g. ~10 kcal/kg/day, lower if very high risk) and increase gradually.
  • Replace electrolytes, and give thiamine / B vitamins (Pabrinex) before/with feeding to prevent Wernicke’s.
  • Do not withhold feeding — correct electrolytes and feed cautiously; stopping feed altogether is not the answer.
🚩
Refeeding syndrome can be fatal (cardiac arrhythmia from hypophosphataemia/hypokalaemia). In high-risk patients: feed cautiously, give thiamine first, and monitor and replace electrolytes daily.
📷 Image placeholder — the refeeding cascade: carbohydrate → insulin → intracellular PO₄/K⁺/Mg²⁺ shift → hypophosphataemia and arrhythmia.
🎓 Exam pearl. Refeeding = insulin-driven intracellular shift of PO₄/K⁺/Mg²⁺ on reintroducing feed. Hypophosphataemia is the hallmark (arrhythmia). High risk: BMI <16, >5 days minimal intake, weight loss, alcohol. Start slow, give thiamine, replace electrolytes.
When assessing cognitive decline, a “dementia screen” of bloods excludes reversible/treatable contributors before diagnosing a neurodegenerative dementia — and delirium and depression must also be excluded.
1The reversible-cause bloods
TFTs (hypothyroidism)Calcium (hyper/hypo)B12 / folateFBC, U&E, LFTsGlucose / HbA1cCRPHIV / syphilis serology (if at risk)
2Why each matters
Hypothyroidism→Reversible cognitive slowing.
Hypercalcaemia→Confusion / cognitive impairment.
B12 / folate deficiency→Cognitive impairment (± neuropathy).
HIV / neurosyphilis→Treatable infective causes.
3Beyond the bloods
  • Exclude delirium (acute, fluctuating) and depression (“pseudodementia”); review medications and alcohol (anticholinergic burden is a common reversible contributor in the elderly). Delirium › / Dementias ›
  • Imaging (CT/MRI) for structural causes (tumour, subdural, normal-pressure hydrocephalus); cognitive testing (MMSE/MoCA/AMTS).
🚩
Rapidly progressive dementia, young onset, or focal neurology → urgent investigation (CJD, autoimmune encephalitis, structural lesion). Normal-pressure hydrocephalus — the triad of dementia, gait apraxia and urinary incontinence — is reversible with shunting.
🎓 Exam pearl. Dementia screen bloods = TFT, calcium, B12/folate, FBC, U&E, LFTs, glucose (± HIV/syphilis) to catch reversible causes. Always exclude delirium and depression. The NPH triad (dementia, gait, incontinence) is reversible.
